what: Every published update of /reports/alpoge-grh.html, newest last. The page prints the newest entry as its 'last updated' line and the list as its change log; its builder refuses to build when the newest entry's count of checks done differs from the record's, so every public update of the count carries a dated line here.

entries.what: First published, as a draft: the archive, the source scan, the readings, the Lean proof that the statement is the textbook RH, the August release re-checked and the bridges compiled are done; the build and the remaining checks are running.

A release timeline at the top, and a title that says what is done and what is next. Amendment A12 adds three checks, each fixed before it runs: a third kernel (con-leche), a re-check on a clean machine, and CHAR, the textbook statements with ζ and the L-functions defined by their series, proved equivalent to the release’s (done). The rule files were submitted for an OpenTimestamps timestamp (its Bitcoin confirmation pending). Two rows now need their own output to count as computed (an outside reading). The build stood at 141,087 of 175,187 files with no error.

Wording made exact after three outside readings: the opening names GRH for Dirichlet L-functions and says what a full pass would and would not mean; of the five theorems, two are about ζ and three about L-functions; the textbook characterisation says ‘analytic continuation’; the amendments are linked and described; a stat for the three kernels. In the record, a check whose step has not run now reads PENDING instead of REFUSED. The build stood at 144,635 of 175,187 files with no error.

After two more readings: the title names RH and GRH; the chain's fourth step names all three kernels (nanoda, Lean’s replay, con-leche) and is decided only when all three are; the route caption no longer says the vacuous items are off the proof, only off the route as drawn (the census will say whether the compiled proof uses them). In the record, a kernel that hits its time limit now reads REFUSED, not PENDING. The build stood at 147,770 of 175,187 files with no error.
The credits name the joint statement of the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative (21 November). The build stood at 172,118 of 175,187 files with no error.

The build passed: Lean compiled all 175,187 files with exit 0 and no sorry, confirmed by a second run with its own exit status, and every source has its compiled file. Mathlib in the workspace equals a clean download (two of Lake’s hash-bookkeeping files differ only in leading zeros of the same number; amendment A14, written after that result and marked so). Our compiled files against Andrew Sutherland’s: 76,968 identical, 98,219 different in bytes; a measurement, not a requirement. Amendment A13 narrowed the statement judge’s precondition to the compiled challenge, after our own disk-saving steps had emptied two non-compiled files; phase 2 restarted. The credits now name the joint statement’s authors correctly.
The axioms: Lean reports that each of the five theorems rests on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and nothing else. The census of the compiled proof is running.

The census of the compiled proof: the five theorems reach 1,478,243 constants in 151,694 modules, the only axioms anywhere in them are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and no constant in the environment has type False. Of the 21 constants J. L. Nielsen’s critique names, 14 are in the compiled proof and 7 are not; the sub-proofs feeding the two key inequalities are traced (closures of 299 to 1,999 constants). The planted errors: Lean’s axiom report names the planted axiom (cheat) in one control and sorryAx in the other, as it must. The statement judge (Comparator) started at 22:27 UTC.

The statement judge (Comparator) could not finish on the build pod: at that pod’s 256 GB memory limit its export stopped making progress, so the run was stopped after 6.2 hours and decides nothing (amendment A17). The same judge now runs on a machine with 376 GB, on a copy of the compiled proof whose 1,226,309 files match the build pod’s hashes. Three planted errors went through the judge on the build pod and were rejected with their diagnostics: a planted axiom, a sorry, a hijacked definition. The export of the proof is written: 61,571,290,481 bytes, with all five theorems in it; a second export, made on the parallel pod, has the same sha256. On that second export nanoda checked 1,484,729 declarations with no type error and rejected the planted error (the Riemann Hypothesis re-typed as False). Those two results are reported beside the registered runs, which have started on the build pod’s own export.

An independent kernel accepts the proof: nanoda, a Lean kernel written in Rust, checked all 1,484,729 declarations of the exported proof with no type error, in 35 minutes. The export holds exactly three axioms: propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice. The planted error for this kernel (the Riemann Hypothesis re-typed as False) is running on the same file. How nanoda’s acceptance line is read was fixed in amendment A18, before this run started.

A third kernel and a second statement judge: con-leche accepted the 1,468,414 declarations of the exported proof in 8 minutes. Its comparison justified each of the five theorems of our challenge file by the release’s export. It rejected both planted errors with their diagnostics: the challenge with 1/2 replaced by 1/3, and the Riemann Hypothesis re-typed as False. nanoda also rejected its planted error on the build pod. The statement judge Comparator is still running on the larger machine, and the clean-machine check has started.

A clean machine agrees. A fresh pod that never ran the release’s code built its own tools and its own copy of our statement file, and received only the exported proof, accepted by its hash. There nanoda checked 1,484,729 declarations with no type error, con-leche’s comparison justified all five theorems, and the three planted errors were rejected. The pod’s own script logged “4 of 5 gates held”: its test for one control misread con-leche’s rejection wording, a fault of our script. The verdict is decided from the five recorded outputs by the rule fixed in advance, and the misread line is kept in the record (amendment A20, made after the result and disclosed as such).

Lean’s own kernel replays the whole proof: leanchecker --fresh Main, starting from an empty environment, checked every module the five theorems rest on and exited 0 after 11 hours 20 minutes on one core. It ran on the parallel pod, on a copy of the compiled proof whose 1,226,309 files match the build pod’s hashes (amendment A15). With nanoda and con-leche, three kernels have now accepted the proof. Left: the statement judge Comparator, its planted-error control and the bridge, all on the larger machine.

The unconditional bridge is closed without a run. The statement judge Comparator has been running for 17.6 hours on the larger machine, and its length puts that bridge at about 20 more hours, above this audit’s budget. By a decision written and published before the judge reported (amendment A21), the bridge is not run now and its row reads REFUSED, for cost. It can be run later as a follow-up. The conditional bridge and the Masullo reading stand as certified. A small script on the machine now makes sure the judge’s control is not started if the judge itself runs out of memory. Left: the statement judge and its planted-error control.

A correction to the page’s wording. After the unconditional bridge was closed at 22:42 UTC, two places still described it as running: the figure of the two releases, and one sentence that read as if the combination had been made. The figure now says “not run”, and the sentence says what is checked (the bound with RH taken as a hypothesis) and what was not run (the two releases in one environment). No row changed.
